cases.name: minimal
cases.note: An empty header and one bare save. The floor of what a bundle is.

cases.name: ps1-card
cases.note: A PS1 card holding three saves, two of them for one game, and a PS2 card holding one save that is itself a directory of files. Between them they cover both nesting shapes a card takes.

cases.name: ps2-card
cases.note: A PS1 card holding three saves, two of them for one game, and a PS2 card holding one save that is itself a directory of files. Between them they cover both nesting shapes a card takes.

cases.name: card-system-entries
cases.note: A PS2 card holding the console's network settings beside a game's save. The settings are no game's, so they are not a save: the directory is one `system` part with an empty payload, and each file in it another, after it.

cases.name: card-image-beside-splits
cases.note: A card-image kept alongside the split saves, which the spec allows so a producer can hold on to the deleted-save residue and free-block contents that splitting drops.

cases.name: card-system-area
cases.note: `system_area` carries the card-level bytes belonging to no save, so a writer can rebuild the card's own identity without a whole card-image. On an N64 pak those bytes are its 32-byte label.

cases.name: card-of-one-game
cases.note: A card holding nothing but saves for one game, which is what Final Fantasy VII does to a PS1 card: one block per save, fifteen slots, no room for anything else. The header names the game, because here a single game really does describe the whole card. The `-Sxx` in the name is the game's own slot and the card's directory slot is a different number, so the two entries below are deliberately not aligned. The outer parts carry no index copy of the game: it would equal the header's, which absence already says.

cases.name: device
cases.note: One console's storage read whole. A Sega CD carries internal backup RAM and a Backup RAM Cart at once; neither is one game's save, and the pair is not a collection, because both came off one system. No card format describes the Sega CD's backup RAM, so each component is a save.

cases.name: collection
cases.note: A collection: no system, no game, no card of its own, and entries that do not agree on a system. This is how one file spans systems, and the PS1 entry is itself a card holding saves.

cases.name: collection-of-devices
cases.note: No depth is written down: a collection can hold a device, which holds a card, which holds saves. Each nested bundle is a shape its holder allows, so the chain ends on its own.

cases.name: device-with-a-clock
cases.note: A console's own clock is on the device, since every game on it reads the one clock and no save holds it. An MVS board's uPD4990A, as ares keeps it: 2001-04-14 12:34:56, a Saturday, beside the board's backup RAM and the card in its slot.

cases.name: n64-device-with-transfer-pak
cases.note: A device's component names the system that reads it. A Game Boy cartridge in an N64's Transfer Pak is a `gb` save in an `n64` device, in the socket `transfer-pak-1`.

cases.name: third-party-kind
cases.note: A kind nobody has to recognize. A consumer treats it as `aux` and hands it back unchanged, which is what lets a producer name one out of a domain it owns instead of registering anything.

cases.name: binding
cases.note: A save the console bound to itself. The bytes are valid and worth keeping, and they will not restore to another console, which is the one thing a consumer cannot work out from the payload.

cases.name: bound-to
cases.note: A save bound to a console and to an account at once, naming both. A consumer compares each identifier byte for byte with its target's, and offers the save to no other.

cases.name: cartridge-and-pak
cases.note: An N64 cartridge beside its Controller Pak is a device of two components, each a nested bundle: the cartridge a save, the pak a card. A note is always a save on a card, so the pak stays a card even where it holds only this game's one note. The cartridge save's own part has the role `cartridge` and carries `x.1sav.n64`, so the save means the same lifted out of the device.

cases.name: n64-chip-unknown
cases.note: A producer that cannot tell a cartridge's chip gives its bytes no `cartridge` part. A 131072-byte file is FlashRAM or 1 Mbit SRAM, so it carries the file whole as `aux`, for a consumer that can tell.

cases.name: n64-state-with-in-game-save
cases.note: An N64 state whose emulator keeps the in-game save beside the core's data. That part is the cartridge's memory, so it has the role `cartridge` and names its chip, as it would in a save of its own.

cases.name: fully-identified
cases.note: Every identification hint at once, plus a populated metadata slot. A real producer emits the hashes it has already computed rather than all four; this is the upper bound, and the only save fixture with a clock reading.

cases.name: save-and-aux
cases.note: A save beside an `aux` part. The thumbnail is no save, so it names its type and rides along for a consumer that wants it.

cases.name: n64-pak-duplicate-note-names
cases.note: An N64 Controller Pak permits two notes with the same game code and note name, so `path` cannot tell them apart and the producer must carry `slot`. This is the case the uniqueness rule exists for, on real hardware.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-eeprom-4k
cases.note: An N64 cartridge save for each chip. The part holding the chip's memory carries `x.1sav.n64`, and its payload is that chip at its full size, from a 4 Kbit EEPROM's 512 bytes to a FlashRAM's 128 KiB.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-eeprom-16k
cases.note: An N64 cartridge save for each chip. The part holding the chip's memory carries `x.1sav.n64`, and its payload is that chip at its full size, from a 4 Kbit EEPROM's 512 bytes to a FlashRAM's 128 KiB.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-sram-256k
cases.note: An N64 cartridge save for each chip. The part holding the chip's memory carries `x.1sav.n64`, and its payload is that chip at its full size, from a 4 Kbit EEPROM's 512 bytes to a FlashRAM's 128 KiB.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-sram-768k
cases.note: An N64 cartridge save for each chip. The part holding the chip's memory carries `x.1sav.n64`, and its payload is that chip at its full size, from a 4 Kbit EEPROM's 512 bytes to a FlashRAM's 128 KiB.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-flash-1m
cases.note: An N64 cartridge save for each chip. The part holding the chip's memory carries `x.1sav.n64`, and its payload is that chip at its full size, from a 4 Kbit EEPROM's 512 bytes to a FlashRAM's 128 KiB.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-sram-1m
cases.note: An N64 cartridge save for each chip. The part holding the chip's memory carries `x.1sav.n64`, and its payload is that chip at its full size, from a 4 Kbit EEPROM's 512 bytes to a FlashRAM's 128 KiB.

cases.name: n64-chip-with-a-later-key
cases.note: The key's integer keys are the spec's, as in the format's own maps. One a later version assigns is ignored and round-tripped, and the chip beside it still fixes the payload's length.

cases.name: n64dd-disk
cases.note: A 64DD disk's save is its RAM area, in block order, and its length is what tells a consumer the disk's type. A type 5 disk's area is its last 204 blocks, 1942080 bytes, the smallest a disk has.

cases.name: nds-card
cases.note: A DS card's save is its chip, whose length is all that tells one chip from another, so it carries no key naming it. Explorers of Sky's 1 Mbit EEPROM is 128 KiB.

cases.name: nds-card-unknown-chip
cases.note: A file whose chip its producer cannot tell, as SkyEmu's 8 MiB is without the game, goes as `aux`, which takes any length.

cases.name: saturn-backup
cases.note: Saturn keeps a save's directory entry at the head of the save's own first block rather than in a directory region, which changes where a reader finds those 30 bytes and not whether they can be carried, so `dirent` holds them like any other format's. What follows them is the block chain, and a writer rewrites that in the payload instead.

cases.name: vmu-card
cases.note: A Dreamcast VMU. Blocks are 512 bytes, so each payload is a run of them, and `capacity` is the whole 131072-byte data area even though only 200 of the card's 256 blocks are ever handed to a save: what fits is capacity minus what the format reserves, which is the writer's arithmetic and not a field here. `system_area` is the card's own colour and icon, which belong to no save on it. The first entry is a mini-game, which runs in place from flash, so a writer puts it back at block 0 and keeps it contiguous; the dirent's type byte is what says so, and this format never reads inside it.

cases.name: neogeo-card
cases.note: A Neo Geo memory card: the smallest card here, 2 KiB of 64-byte blocks behind a 4-byte directory entry. The entry holds no name, only a sub-number, the game's NGH number and the save's first block, so `path` spells the first two: `0201-0` is Metal Slug's save 0. The blocks are after the five the card reserves for itself. `system_area` is the card's 64-byte header block, which carries the cardholder username and the region of the console that formatted it, belonging to the card rather than to anything saved on it.

cases.name: n64-note-with-extension
cases.note: An N64 note can carry an extension beside its 16-byte name. `path` joins the two with a dot, each decoded through the pak's own character table.

cases.name: gc-card
cases.note: A GameCube Memory Card 59: 64 blocks of 8192 bytes, named for the 59 left once the header, the directory and the block allocation table have taken theirs, and `capacity` is all 64 of them. Taken from a real `.gci`, which is a 64-byte dirent followed by the payload and nothing else: `GFZE` plus `8P` for the serial, `f_zero.dat` for the path, and 32768 bytes of save, which is the four blocks the dirent claims. That is the block count being derivable rather than stored. The same dirent gives the save's first block as 5, the first block a GameCube card has free, and this format drops that number on the floor: it is true of the card it was read from and of no other. F-Zero GX also signs its save against the destination card's flash serial and refuses one that does not match, so a writer re-signs it on arrival rather than copying the payload untouched.

cases.name: ps1-multi-block-save
cases.note: A PS1 save spanning two blocks is one part of 16384 bytes. The card allocated two blocks and they may not have been adjacent, which is not recorded: block placement is the destination allocator's business.

cases.name: transfer-pak
cases.note: A Transfer Pak puts a Game Boy cartridge in an N64 controller, and Pokemon Stadium writes that cartridge's SRAM. The save is `gb` because that is what will load it; the N64 is provenance, which is what `source` is for.

cases.name: empty-formatted-card
cases.note: A formatted card with nothing saved on it. The card is real and worth carrying, and a `card_image` is the only part it can have, since there is no save to nest.

cases.name: zero-byte-payload
cases.note: A zero-length payload. A save slot a console formatted and never wrote to is still a part, and sha256 over no bytes is perfectly well defined.

cases.name: token-bound-save
cases.note: An amiibo: a few hundred bytes on an NFC tag, signed against that tag's own serial. No `system`, because several consoles read one and none of them owns it, which is a case the optional header is there for. `binding` is `medium` rather than `device`: any console can write it and the result stays valid, but copying it to a second tag does not.

cases.name: high-numbered-socket
cases.note: A numbered socket past anything the registry enumerates. Eight VMU slots across four Dreamcast controllers, and the prefix is what a consumer matches on, so a VMU read from `memcard-8` is understood without that role being listed.

cases.name: source-provenance
cases.note: Provenance at both levels: a cartridge reader assembled the bundle, and one part came from an emulator instead, so it carries its own source. Note the split inside one map: `device_kind` is a spec slug nobody may mint into, while `app` beside it is the producer's own name, here reverse-DNS for the reader and an Apps registry slug for the emulator. The reader runs no core; the emulator names the one it ran in `core`, and the firmware it ran on in `platform`.

cases.name: source-utc-offset
cases.note: A MiSTer stamps a clock's anchor in local standard time counted as though it were UTC, and says how far that is from UTC: Pacific time, eight hours west, a negative integer on the wire.

cases.name: game-ids
cases.note: Catalog ids, keyed by resolver name. A producer aligned with several catalogs records one entry each, and the id is whatever form that catalog publishes: an integer for one, a string for the next.

cases.name: part-extension-keys
cases.note: Extension keys sit flat on the header and on a part alike, named by reversing a domain the producer holds or by taking a reserved name in the `x` tree when the value belongs to no one producer. Both kinds ride here.

cases.name: game-extension-keys
cases.note: `game` takes extension keys too, for a clue none of its integer keys names. A cartridge reader that read only the ROM header has a serial and a title and no hash, and the header's revision byte beside them is what tells two releases sharing that serial apart. A consumer that does not recognise the key skips it when matching and hands it back unchanged.

cases.name: state-minimal
cases.note: A save state at its smallest: the core it loads into, and the core's own data. A state with no game, no time and no screenshot still loads where it was taken, so nothing else is required.

cases.name: state-retroarch
cases.note: A RetroArch state in slot 3, with the screenshot RetroArch keeps beside it. The state part is the RASTATE file's memory block, unwrapped and decompressed. The achievement block is RetroArch's own and opaque, so it rides as an `aux` part named for the block it came from.

cases.name: state-with-in-game-save
cases.note: mGBA's own state file is a PNG: its image is the screenshot, and its chunks carry the core's data and the in-game save beside it. Split, that is a state part, a screenshot, and an ordinary save part, which a consumer can lift into a save bundle of its own. The cartridge's clock stays inside the core's data, and the two clock keys are a reading of it, which that lifted save takes with it. The player's cheats ride on the state part, and stay behind when the save is lifted.

cases.name: state-auto
cases.note: The state an emulator writes on its own to resume from, as RetroArch's `.state.auto` is. Neither it nor its screenshot has a slot, which is fine: no two parts of one kind share an address, and these are two kinds.

cases.name: state-undo
cases.note: A state the emulator kept so a player can take back a save: what slot 2 held before it was overwritten. Without a slot, an undo state is the game just before a load.

cases.name: state-taken-with
cases.note: Everything a state can record about what it was taken with: the host's byte order and word size, the BIOS the machine booted, the machine's language setting and the core's options.

cases.name: state-duckstation
cases.note: A DuckStation state lifted out of its file. The version DuckStation stamps in its own header goes in `format_version`, since the core's data no longer carries it. The producer could not tell which BIOS the machine booted, which null says; leaving the key out would say there was none.

cases.name: screenshot
cases.note: A screenshot on its own, linked to its game and the emulator that took it. PPSSPP writes JPEG, and it stays JPEG: encoding it again could not get back what the first encode dropped.

cases.name: collection-of-one-game
cases.note: One game's in-game save beside a state and a screenshot of it. Each stays a bundle of its own, so the in-game save's content hash does not move every time a state is taken, and a collection is what puts them in one file.

cases.name: part-unknown-integer-key
cases.note: An integer key nobody has assigned yet, on a part and on the header.

cases.name: header-unknown-integer-key
cases.note: An integer key nobody has assigned yet, on a part and on the header.

cases.name: shape-unknown
cases.note: A shape this version does not define. A decoder keeps the bundle, and declines anything that depends on knowing what the shape means.

cases.name: card-format-unknown
cases.note: A card format this version does not list. A consumer keeps the card and declines to write it, since it cannot rebuild what it cannot read.

cases.name: kind-unknown
cases.note: A new name in each of the other lists the spec owns. A kind the decoder does not know is handled as `aux`; the rest are labels it carries.

cases.name: binding-unknown
cases.note: A new name in each of the other lists the spec owns. A kind the decoder does not know is handled as `aux`; the rest are labels it carries.

cases.name: origin-unknown
cases.note: A new name in each of the other lists the spec owns. A kind the decoder does not know is handled as `aux`; the rest are labels it carries.

cases.name: device-kind-unknown
cases.note: A new name in each of the other lists the spec owns. A kind the decoder does not know is handled as `aux`; the rest are labels it carries.

cases.name: header-without-shape
cases.note: `shape` says which document governs the bundle, so it is the one header key that is never optional and never inferred.

cases.name: shape-as-integer
cases.note: `shape` says which document governs the bundle, so it is the one header key that is never optional and never inferred.

cases.name: card-without-card-map
cases.note: Each shape admits a different header. A card is a card because it carries the `card` map, a save never carries one, and a collection has nothing of its own to say.

cases.name: save-with-card-map
cases.note: Each shape admits a different header. A card is a card because it carries the `card` map, a save never carries one, and a collection has nothing of its own to say.

cases.name: collection-with-system
cases.note: Each shape admits a different header. A card is a card because it carries the `card` map, a save never carries one, and a collection has nothing of its own to say.

cases.name: collection-with-game
cases.note: Each shape admits a different header. A card is a card because it carries the `card` map, a save never carries one, and a collection has nothing of its own to say.

cases.name: collection-with-card-map
cases.note: Each shape admits a different header. A card is a card because it carries the `card` map, a save never carries one, and a collection has nothing of its own to say.

cases.name: device-without-system
cases.note: `system` is what tells a device from a collection, so it is required, and the components hold saves for many games rather than for one.

cases.name: device-with-game
cases.note: `system` is what tells a device from a collection, so it is required, and the components hold saves for many games rather than for one.

cases.name: device-with-card-map
cases.note: `system` is what tells a device from a collection, so it is required, and the components hold saves for many games rather than for one.

cases.name: card-without-capacity
cases.note: `card` needs both format and capacity; neither is optional.

cases.name: dirent-as-text
cases.note: `dirent` is a byte string. Text would make it look parseable, which is the one thing this spec promises it is not.

cases.name: kind-as-integer
cases.note: `kind` is text. An integer here would be a producer reaching for the old tag numbers, which no longer mean anything.

cases.name: empty-parts
cases.note: A bundle with nothing in it. Every other container in the format forbids its own empty form, and a bundle holding no part carries no save.

cases.name: path-spelled-empty
cases.note: A default written out, which would give one part several encodings. Each of the three is written by leaving its key out.

cases.name: kind-spelled-save
cases.note: A default written out, which would give one part several encodings. Each of the three is written by leaving its key out.

cases.name: role-spelled-primary
cases.note: A default written out, which would give one part several encodings. Each of the three is written by leaving its key out.

cases.name: role-with-underscore
cases.note: A slug has no `_`. A name that breaks the grammar is malformed rather than a later version's, since nobody could have assigned it.

cases.name: kind-with-underscore
cases.note: A slug has no `_`. A name that breaks the grammar is malformed rather than a later version's, since nobody could have assigned it.

cases.name: slug-with-doubled-dash
cases.note: A slug separates runs with a single dash and carries none at either end, so a doubled or dangling one is malformed rather than an odd name.

cases.name: slug-with-trailing-dash
cases.note: A slug separates runs with a single dash and carries none at either end, so a doubled or dangling one is malformed rather than an odd name.

cases.name: slug-too-long
cases.note: A slug runs to 64 bytes at most. This one is 65.

cases.name: role-with-uppercase
cases.note: A slug is lowercase, separates its runs with `-` and holds no `_`, in every field that takes one. A value written any other way is malformed rather than a later version's: round-tripping applies to names this decoder has not heard of, not to names that could not have been assigned.

cases.name: system-slug-with-underscore
cases.note: A slug is lowercase, separates its runs with `-` and holds no `_`, in every field that takes one. A value written any other way is malformed rather than a later version's: round-tripping applies to names this decoder has not heard of, not to names that could not have been assigned.

cases.name: game-system-with-underscore
cases.note: A slug is lowercase, separates its runs with `-` and holds no `_`, in every field that takes one. A value written any other way is malformed rather than a later version's: round-tripping applies to names this decoder has not heard of, not to names that could not have been assigned.

cases.name: game-system-as-integer
cases.note: A slug is lowercase, separates its runs with `-` and holds no `_`, in every field that takes one. A value written any other way is malformed rather than a later version's: round-tripping applies to names this decoder has not heard of, not to names that could not have been assigned.

cases.name: card-format-with-underscore
cases.note: A slug is lowercase, separates its runs with `-` and holds no `_`, in every field that takes one. A value written any other way is malformed rather than a later version's: round-tripping applies to names this decoder has not heard of, not to names that could not have been assigned.

cases.name: card-format-reverse-dns
cases.note: A card format is spec-owned, and a producer may not mint one. An unknown format leaves a consumer unable to write the card back at all, so a reverse-DNS name here is malformed rather than a private extension.

cases.name: device-kind-reverse-dns
cases.note: A device kind is spec-owned too, so a minted one is malformed. `app` in the same map names the producer itself and is minted freely, so the two fields of that map pull in opposite directions.

cases.name: core-as-library-name
cases.note: A core's slug derives from the name RetroArch reports, and is not that name. `mGBA` is the core's `library_name` verbatim, which fails the slug arm on case and the reverse-DNS arm for having no dot, so it is malformed rather than a core nobody has listed yet.

cases.name: platform-as-display-name
cases.note: The same for a platform written the way it writes its own name. `muOS` is a display name, not a slug, and has no dot to be a minted one.

cases.name: utc-offset-out-of-range
cases.note: An offset is the span real zones occupy, -12:00 through +14:00. A day east is no zone at all, and one a consumer would move a clock by.

cases.name: utc-offset-zero
cases.note: Zero is UTC, and anchors on UTC are written by leaving the key out.

cases.name: role-reverse-dns
cases.note: A role takes a registry slug and never a minted name. A socket is hardware and belongs to nobody, and a private name for one could not be matched against a target by anything but its author, which is the whole job the field does.

cases.name: binding-reverse-dns
cases.note: A binding names a category everyone shares, so it is spec-owned too. A private one would split the category instead of extending it, leaving a consumer unable to tell a device binding from an account one.

cases.name: kind-dotted-but-not-reverse-dns
cases.note: A dotted name is a producer's own and therefore has to be a well-formed reverse-DNS name, which forbids `_` in a label. Failing both arms is the point: this is neither a spec slug nor a name anybody could hold.

cases.name: path-too-long
cases.note: `path` is capped so a consumer can size the head region. 512 is the limit, in bytes rather than characters, since that is what a decoder can check.

cases.name: path-leading-slash
cases.note: A path is relative, `/` separates its segments, and no segment is empty, `.` or `..`. Each of these is a second spelling of an address, or one that climbs out of the container it names.

cases.name: path-trailing-slash
cases.note: A path is relative, `/` separates its segments, and no segment is empty, `.` or `..`. Each of these is a second spelling of an address, or one that climbs out of the container it names.

cases.name: path-empty-segment
cases.note: A path is relative, `/` separates its segments, and no segment is empty, `.` or `..`. Each of these is a second spelling of an address, or one that climbs out of the container it names.

cases.name: path-dot-segment
cases.note: A path is relative, `/` separates its segments, and no segment is empty, `.` or `..`. Each of these is a second spelling of an address, or one that climbs out of the container it names.

cases.name: path-dot-dot-segment
cases.note: A path is relative, `/` separates its segments, and no segment is empty, `.` or `..`. Each of these is a second spelling of an address, or one that climbs out of the container it names.

cases.name: resolver-name-not-reverse-dns
cases.note: A resolver name is minted exactly as an extension key is, so a bare word fails for the same reason: nothing says whose catalog this id is from.

cases.name: extension-key-not-reverse-dns
cases.note: An extension key is a reverse-DNS name or it is nothing. Without that there is no way to tell whose key this is, which is the one thing the namespace buys. A bare word and an uppercase name are both unmintable, in `game` as much as on the header or a part.

cases.name: extension-key-uppercase
cases.note: An extension key is a reverse-DNS name or it is nothing. Without that there is no way to tell whose key this is, which is the one thing the namespace buys. A bare word and an uppercase name are both unmintable, in `game` as much as on the header or a part.

cases.name: extension-key-too-long
cases.note: A reverse-DNS name runs to 255 characters, as a domain does. This one has 256, every label within its own limit.

cases.name: game-extension-key-not-reverse-dns
cases.note: A reverse-DNS name runs to 255 characters, as a domain does. This one has 256, every label within its own limit.

cases.name: bundled-at-as-float
cases.note: Tag 1 admits a float and this format does not. Left open, one instant would have two conforming encodings and the content hash would stop being a function of what the bundle says.

cases.name: state-without-source
cases.note: A state only loads into the core that took it, so its header has to say which: a core, or the app where nothing runs one.

cases.name: state-source-without-core-or-app
cases.note: A state only loads into the core that took it, so its header has to say which: a core, or the app where nothing runs one.

cases.name: state-part-in-a-save
cases.note: A state part and a screenshot part sit only in the shapes that hold them, so a consumer restoring an in-game save never meets either.

cases.name: screenshot-part-in-a-save
cases.note: A state part and a screenshot part sit only in the shapes that hold them, so a consumer restoring an in-game save never meets either.

cases.name: state-part-with-content-type
cases.note: A state part is the core's own data, which has no media type to name.

cases.name: screenshot-without-content-type
cases.note: A screenshot names its image type, and the type is one every consumer can show. Anything else is encoded as PNG on the way in.

cases.name: screenshot-as-webp
cases.note: A screenshot names its image type, and the type is one every consumer can show. Anything else is encoded as PNG on the way in.

cases.name: screenshot-with-two-images
cases.note: A screenshot bundle is one image. Two images are two bundles, which a collection can hold together.

cases.name: screenshot-holding-a-save
cases.note: A screenshot bundle is one image. Two images are two bundles, which a collection can hold together.

cases.name: system-part-in-a-save
cases.note: A `system` part is an entry on a card that belongs to no game, so it sits on a card and nowhere else, says where on the card it goes, and names no game.

cases.name: system-part-without-path
cases.note: A `system` part is an entry on a card that belongs to no game, so it sits on a card and nowhere else, says where on the card it goes, and names no game.

cases.name: system-part-naming-a-game
cases.note: A `system` part is an entry on a card that belongs to no game, so it sits on a card and nowhere else, says where on the card it goes, and names no game.

cases.name: taken-at-on-a-save
cases.note: `taken_at` is when a state or a screenshot was taken, which an in-game save has no field for. `taken_with` and `origin` belong to a state alone.

cases.name: taken-with-on-a-screenshot
cases.note: `taken_at` is when a state or a screenshot was taken, which an in-game save has no field for. `taken_with` and `origin` belong to a state alone.

cases.name: origin-on-a-save
cases.note: `taken_at` is when a state or a screenshot was taken, which an in-game save has no field for. `taken_with` and `origin` belong to a state alone.

cases.name: origin-reverse-dns
cases.note: An origin names a category everyone shares, so like a binding it is spec-owned, and a minted one is malformed.

cases.name: byte-order-unknown
cases.note: Each `taken_with` entry takes only its own values, so that one setting has one spelling. A byte order is little or big and a word size 32 or 64 bits. A format version is a number, never the text a file writes it as. A language tag is in BCP 47's own case, with the language in lower case.

A format version is a number, never the text a file writes it as. A language tag is in BCP 47's own case, with the language in lower case.

cases.note: Each `taken_with` entry takes only its own values, so that one setting has one spelling. A byte order is little or big and a word size 32 or 64 bits. A format version is a number, never the text a file writes it as. A language tag is in BCP 47's own case, with the language in lower case.

A format version is a number, never the text a file writes it as. A language tag is in BCP 47's own case, with the language in lower case.

cases.name: empty-game
cases.note: An optional map, text or byte string is absent rather than empty: an empty one is a second spelling of absence.

cases.name: empty-part-game
cases.note: An optional map, text or byte string is absent rather than empty: an empty one is a second spelling of absence.

cases.name: empty-source
cases.note: An optional map, text or byte string is absent rather than empty: an empty one is a second spelling of absence.

cases.name: empty-taken-with
cases.note: An optional map, text or byte string is absent rather than empty: an empty one is a second spelling of absence.

cases.name: empty-description
cases.note: An optional map, text or byte string is absent rather than empty: an empty one is a second spelling of absence.

cases.name: empty-serial
cases.note: An optional map, text or byte string is absent rather than empty: an empty one is a second spelling of absence.

cases.name: empty-dirent
cases.note: An optional map, text or byte string is absent rather than empty: an empty one is a second spelling of absence.

cases.name: empty-core-options
cases.note: Empty maps, which absence already encodes.

cases.name: empty-firmware
cases.note: Empty maps, which absence already encodes.

cases.name: rom-hash-wrong-length
cases.note: A digest has to match the length its algorithm tag implies, and the tag has to be one of the four the shared type defines. Neither is recoverable by guessing, so both are malformed rather than skippable.

cases.name: rom-hash-unknown-tag
cases.note: A digest has to match the length its algorithm tag implies, and the tag has to be one of the four the shared type defines. Neither is recoverable by guessing, so both are malformed rather than skippable.

cases.name: empty-rom-hashes
cases.note: Empty containers, which absence already encodes.

cases.name: empty-game-id
cases.note: Empty containers, which absence already encodes.

cases.name: part-sha256-wrong-length
cases.note: A part's sha256 is exactly 32 bytes; the spec pins the algorithm, so a shorter digest is a different algorithm smuggled in without its tag.

cases.name: part-sha256-untagged
cases.note: The tag is what lets a generic reader name the digest, so an untagged one is not a hash value at all. A different algorithm's tag is rejected too: this spec pins sha256 here so that identity has exactly one answer.

cases.name: part-sha256-wrong-algorithm
cases.note: The tag is what lets a generic reader name the digest, so an untagged one is not a hash value at all. A different algorithm's tag is rejected too: this spec pins sha256 here so that identity has exactly one answer.

cases.name: payload-at-old-key-8
cases.note: A pre-renumber bundle, from when the payload sat in the unsigned range. Key 11 is `game` now, and the payload is at -1, so this is rejected rather than read as a game map.

cases.name: save-holding-a-bundle-part
cases.note: A save holds no nested bundle: a component that is a card of its own makes the bundle a device. A state holds none either: a state and an in-game save in one file is a collection of two bundles.

cases.name: state-holding-a-bundle-part
cases.note: A save holds no nested bundle: a component that is a card of its own makes the bundle a device. A state holds none either: a state and an in-game save in one file is a collection of two bundles.

cases.name: card-holding-a-bare-save
cases.note: A card's own parts are its saves, each nested, and the entries beside them. A bare save part on a card is a save flattened out of the bundle it belongs in.

cases.name: device-component-without-role
cases.note: A device's component sits in a socket, and the role is the whole of what tells two components apart, so it is required.

cases.name: bundle-part-with-content-type
cases.note: A `bundle` part's media type is this format's by construction, so it names none. It names no binding either: that belongs on the part inside holding the bound bytes.

cases.name: bundle-part-with-binding
cases.note: A `bundle` part's media type is this format's by construction, so it names none. It names no binding either: that belongs on the part inside holding the bound bytes.

cases.name: system-on-a-plain-part
cases.note: Part key 12 is an index copy of a nested bundle's `system`, so it sits on a `bundle` part and nowhere else.

cases.name: card-image-naming-a-game
cases.note: A whole card belongs to no one game, so a `card-image` names none.

cases.name: bound-to-without-binding
cases.note: `bound_to` comes only with `binding`, and holds only the identifiers its value names: a console's for `device`, never an account's.

cases.name: bound-to-naming-another-target
cases.note: `bound_to` comes only with `binding`, and holds only the identifiers its value names: a console's for `device`, never an account's.

cases.name: trailing-byte
cases.note: The file is one tagged item and nothing else. Trailing bytes, the self-describe tag in front, or no bundle tag at all each make it something other than a bundle.

cases.name: self-describe-tag
cases.note: The file is one tagged item and nothing else. Trailing bytes, the self-describe tag in front, or no bundle tag at all each make it something other than a bundle.

cases.name: untagged
cases.note: The file is one tagged item and nothing else. Trailing bytes, the self-describe tag in front, or no bundle tag at all each make it something other than a bundle.

cases.name: indefinite-length-parts
cases.note: 9f/ff is an indefinite-length array. Definite lengths everywhere is the first thing 4.2 requires, and an encoder that streams without knowing its length ahead of time produces this without meaning to.

cases.name: indefinite-length-part-map
cases.note: 9f/ff is an indefinite-length array. Definite lengths everywhere is the first thing 4.2 requires, and an encoder that streams without knowing its length ahead of time produces this without meaning to.

cases.name: non-preferred-key-head
cases.note: 18 00 encodes 0 in two bytes where 00 does it in one. Preferred serialization means the shortest head that fits, and a library that always writes a fixed width emits this.

cases.name: non-preferred-value-head
cases.note: 18 00 encodes 0 in two bytes where 00 does it in one. Preferred serialization means the shortest head that fits, and a library that always writes a fixed width emits this.

cases.name: map-keys-out-of-order
cases.note: Keys sort by the bytewise order of their encodings. Here 9 precedes 0, which decodes to the same map and hashes differently.

cases.name: duplicate-map-key
cases.note: Two entries for key 0. A decoder that keeps the last one and a decoder that keeps the first disagree about what the bundle says.

cases.name: indefinite-length-payload
cases.note: A byte string has a definite length too. 5f/ff is the payload sent in two chunks, which decodes to the same four bytes.

cases.name: non-preferred-length-head
cases.note: A length is a head like any other, so it takes the shortest form that fits. A streaming encoder that reserves four bytes for a length writes this.

cases.name: parts-out-of-order
cases.note: Parts sit in strictly ascending `id` order. This one holds id 1 then id 0, which decodes to the same two parts and hashes differently. The parts sit in different slots, so nothing else about them is wrong.

cases.name: parts-share-an-id
cases.note: Strictly ascending means no two parts share an `id`, so nothing says which of the two an extension key names.

cases.name: text-not-nfc
cases.note: Text is in NFC. "Pokémon" written with a combining acute (U+0065 U+0301) rather than the precomposed é (U+00E9) is the same string to a reader and a different one to a hash. Real catalogues carry both forms.

cases.name: rom-hashes-out-of-order
cases.note: Hash values sort ascending by tag, so sha1 (18542) after sha256 (18540). Reversed here.

cases.name: rom-hashes-duplicate-algorithm
cases.note: At most one entry per algorithm. Two sha256 digests name two different files, and nothing says which one the bundle means.

cases.name: firmware-hashes-out-of-order
cases.note: The ordering rule holds for every list of hash values, a firmware file's in `taken_with` as much as `rom_hashes`.

cases.name: nested-bundle-not-canonical
cases.note: The encoding rules hold at every depth. This card's save sets its part's `id` in two bytes where one does, and the outer `sha256` is over those bytes, so only the encoding is wrong.

cases.name: bundle-part-payload-not-a-bundle
cases.note: A `bundle` part's payload has to decode as a bundle at all, and as a shape its holder may hold. This one is a plain save's bytes.

cases.name: collection-in-a-collection
cases.note: A collection never holds another collection.

cases.name: card-holding-a-card
cases.note: A card holds saves and nothing nested beyond them, and a device holds cards and saves.

cases.name: device-holding-a-collection
cases.note: A card holds saves and nothing nested beyond them, and a device holds cards and saves.

cases.name: device-holding-a-state
cases.note: A card holds saves and nothing nested beyond them, and a device holds cards and saves.

cases.name: nested-save-spelling-out-a-default
cases.note: One bad part makes the whole bundle malformed, however deep it sits. The card and its first save are fine; the second save writes out a default, so the card is malformed too, and a decoder keeps neither save.

cases.name: part-sha256-mismatch
cases.note: A part's `sha256` is the digest of its payload. Here it names other bytes, so a decoder handing the payload out would hand out something corrupt.

cases.name: bundle-part-sha256-mismatch
cases.note: The outer sha256 is the inner bundle's identity, which is what makes extracting a save a byte copy. Here it names bytes the payload is not.

cases.name: parts-share-an-address
cases.note: No two parts may agree on `role`, `path` and `slot` together, and with all three defaulting to absence two bare parts collide on every one of them. That is a bundle a consumer cannot name a part in, or match against a target, so it cannot act on it at all.

cases.name: device-components-share-a-role
cases.note: A device's components never share a role, whatever else tells them apart. These two differ in `path`, which the ordinary addressing rule would allow.

cases.name: part-game-equal-to-header
cases.note: A part's `game` that equals the header's is a default spelled out, since a part with none takes the header's. On a card of one game, that makes an index copy on each save's part a second spelling of the same card.

cases.name: card-of-one-game-with-index-copies
cases.note: A part's `game` that equals the header's is a default spelled out, since a part with none takes the header's. On a card of one game, that makes an index copy on each save's part a second spelling of the same card.

cases.name: card-parts-disagree-on-role
cases.note: Every part of one card names the same socket, or none does: a card sat in one slot when it was read.

cases.name: state-without-a-state-part
cases.note: A state bundle holds exactly one state part. Without one there is nothing to load, and with two a consumer cannot tell which one the bundle is.

cases.name: state-with-two-state-parts
cases.note: A state bundle holds exactly one state part. Without one there is nothing to load, and with two a consumer cannot tell which one the bundle is.

cases.name: state-with-two-screenshots
cases.note: And at most one screenshot, since the screenshot is the state's picture. A screenshot part takes no `role`, `path` or `slot`, so two of them also share an address: a decoder may catch this by either rule.

cases.name: system-file-without-its-directory
cases.note: A `system` file sits in a directory that has a `system` part of its own, ahead of the file's, so a writer has made the directory before it reaches the file. Here the directory is missing, and then it comes too late.

cases.name: system-file-before-its-directory
cases.note: A `system` file sits in a directory that has a `system` part of its own, ahead of the file's, so a writer has made the directory before it reaches the file. Here the directory is missing, and then it comes too late.

cases.name: neogeo-path-uppercase
cases.note: A Neo Geo save's `path` is its NGH number in four lowercase hex digits, a dash, then its sub-number in one more. Sub-number 10 is `a` and NGH 201 is `0201`, so neither of these is how a producer spells them.

cases.name: neogeo-path-unpadded
cases.note: A Neo Geo save's `path` is its NGH number in four lowercase hex digits, a dash, then its sub-number in one more. Sub-number 10 is `a` and NGH 201 is `0201`, so neither of these is how a producer spells them.

cases.name: dirent-wrong-length
cases.note: A `dirent` is as long as its card's format makes it. A Neo Geo entry is four bytes, and this one stops at three. A PS1 entry is 128 bytes, and this one is 127.

cases.name: ps1-dirent-wrong-length
cases.note: A `dirent` is as long as its card's format makes it. A Neo Geo entry is four bytes, and this one stops at three. A PS1 entry is 128 bytes, and this one is 127.

cases.name: neogeo-system-area-only-the-username
cases.note: A Neo Geo card's `system_area` is its whole 64-byte header block, which carries the cardholder username and the card's region. The username alone is 16 bytes and leaves the region behind.

cases.name: n64-path-outside-the-table
cases.note: An N64 note's `path` is its name decoded through the pak's character table, which has no lowercase letters. So this spelling cannot have come from a note, and a producer leaves `path` out rather than invent one.

cases.name: n64-path-longer-than-a-note-name
cases.note: A note's name is 16 bytes, so its spelling runs to 16 characters at most before any extension. This one has 17 and no extension. Its extension is 4 bytes, so the next one has 5 after the dot.

cases.name: n64-path-extension-too-long
cases.note: A note's name is 16 bytes, so its spelling runs to 16 characters at most before any extension. This one has 17 and no extension. Its extension is 4 bytes, so the next one has 5 after the dot.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-wrong-size
cases.note: An N64 cartridge's chip fixes how long its payload is. A 16 Kbit EEPROM is 2048 bytes, and this payload is the 512 of a 4 Kbit one, which is the mix-up the key is there to prevent.

cases.name: n64-chip-undefined
cases.note: The chip names count kilobits, as the chips are sold. This one counts the payload in KiB instead, so it is no chip the key's page lists, and a consumer could not say how long the save should be.

cases.name: n64-chip-not-a-map
cases.note: The value is a map whose key 0 names the chip. A bare name is not one.

cases.name: n64-cartridge-without-its-chip
cases.note: The `cartridge` part of an N64 save says which chip it holds. Neither the bytes nor their length can say it for the part.

cases.name: n64-device-cartridge-without-its-chip
cases.note: The same inside a device and inside a state. The part has the role `cartridge` in a bundle naming `n64`, so it is marked as a cartridge's however deep it sits and whatever shape holds it.

cases.name: n64-state-cartridge-without-its-chip
cases.note: The same inside a device and inside a state. The part has the role `cartridge` in a bundle naming `n64`, so it is marked as a cartridge's however deep it sits and whatever shape holds it.

cases.name: n64-chip-on-the-header
cases.note: The key goes on the part holding the chip's memory and nowhere else. A header, the `bundle` part wrapping a device's cartridge save, a note's own save, a `game` map and a Game Boy cartridge's part each hold something other than an N64 chip.

cases.name: n64-chip-on-a-bundle-part
cases.note: The key goes on the part holding the chip's memory and nowhere else. A header, the `bundle` part wrapping a device's cartridge save, a note's own save, a `game` map and a Game Boy cartridge's part each hold something other than an N64 chip.

cases.name: n64-chip-on-a-note
cases.note: The key goes on the part holding the chip's memory and nowhere else. A header, the `bundle` part wrapping a device's cartridge save, a note's own save, a `game` map and a Game Boy cartridge's part each hold something other than an N64 chip.

cases.name: n64-chip-in-a-game-map
cases.note: The key goes on the part holding the chip's memory and nowhere else. A header, the `bundle` part wrapping a device's cartridge save, a note's own save, a `game` map and a Game Boy cartridge's part each hold something other than an N64 chip.

cases.name: n64-chip-on-a-gb-cartridge
cases.note: The key goes on the part holding the chip's memory and nowhere else. A header, the `bundle` part wrapping a device's cartridge save, a note's own save, a `game` map and a Game Boy cartridge's part each hold something other than an N64 chip.

cases.name: n64-two-cartridge-parts
cases.note: A cartridge has one save chip, so a bundle naming `n64` holds one `cartridge` part at most. These two differ only in `path`.

cases.name: n64-note-as-a-save-part
cases.note: A Controller Pak is a card, and a note is a save on it. No part of a save names a card's slot, so a note beside the cartridge's part is a save flattened out of the card it belongs on.

cases.name: n64dd-disk-with-a-role
cases.note: A 64DD disk's save holds its RAM area in one `save` part with no role, which is how a decoder finds it. A role, or a second save part, leaves it unable to tell which bytes are the area.

cases.name: n64dd-disk-with-two-save-parts
cases.note: A 64DD disk's save holds its RAM area in one `save` part with no role, which is how a decoder finds it. A role, or a second save part, leaves it unable to tell which bytes are the area.

cases.name: n64dd-disk-wrong-size
cases.note: A 64DD disk's save is the whole of its RAM area, which no disk type makes 32 KiB long. A save of part of the area cannot be told from a disk of another type.

cases.name: nds-card-wrong-size
cases.note: A DS card's save is as long as one of its chips. 8314 bytes is an 8 KiB EEPROM with DeSmuME's footer still on, which no card holds.
